## Goal

Use BLAST to identify or interpret an unknown sequence, then document the search so that someone else could audit it.

## Provided query

If you do not yet have a project sequence, use the practice fish COI query in [provided-query.fasta](provided-query.fasta). Everyone can complete the workflow with it before project data are settled.

```text
>week01_unknown_fish_coi_practice

```

## Tasks

1. Save the query as `data/processed/week01/query.fasta`. It is a small file you made, not a raw download, so it belongs under `data/processed/` and is fine to commit (`data/raw/` stays ignored).
2. Run a BLAST search with NCBI web BLAST, or command-line BLAST on Raven if you already have it working.
3. Save the top-hit table or downloaded results under `output/week01/`.
4. In your notebook entry, report the database searched, top hit, percent identity, query coverage, e-value, and whether the result makes biological sense.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Web BLAST in 6 steps

1. Go to [NCBI BLAST](https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) and click **Nucleotide BLAST**.
2. Paste the whole query, header line included, into **Enter Query Sequence**. Give the search a title, such as `week01 COI practice`.
3. Under **Choose Search Set**, keep **Standard databases** and choose the core nucleotide database (`core_nt`; older pages call it `nt`). Leave **Organism** blank so the search is not biased toward a group you already expect.
4. Under **Program Selection**, keep **Highly similar sequences (megablast)**, which fits a COI barcode. Click **BLAST**. Results usually take under a minute; leave the tab open.
5. On the results page, stay on the **Descriptions** tab. Click **Download** and choose **Hit Table (CSV)**. Save it as `output/week01/blast-hits.csv`. Write down the **RID** shown at the top and today's date.
6. Look past the first row. Compare the top five to ten hits for percent identity, query coverage, and organism, and click a hit to see its alignment. This is the evidence for your interpretation.
:::

## In your project

If you already have a sequence from your own project (a transcript, contig, marker, or amplicon), BLAST it too and report the same fields. Note whether sequence similarity, annotation, or database choice is going to matter for your project. This becomes part of your proposal.

## Interpretation checklist

Your entry should make the search auditable:

- Query file and sequence length.
- BLAST program used (`blastn`, `blastx`, or NCBI web BLAST).
- Database searched and date searched.
- Top hit accession, description, and organism.
- Percent identity, query coverage, alignment length, and e-value.
- Whether the next few hits support the same interpretation.
- One caveat: short marker length, close congeners, incomplete references, contamination, or database bias.

## Database choice

- For broad DNA identification, start with NCBI `nt`.
- For COI barcodes, compare NCBI results with what a barcode-focused database such as BOLD would give.
- For transcripts or contigs that may encode proteins, consider whether `blastx` against a protein database is more informative than nucleotide BLAST.
- For eDNA-style markers, note whether the marker is long and variable enough for species-level claims.

## The one pull request

This is the only week that requires a pull request. Fork the [course repository](https://github.com/sr320/course-fish546-2026), add one line to `roster.md` with your name, your repository link, and your project track, and open a pull request. We review and merge them together in Thursday's session. After this week, all of your work goes directly into your own repository.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Fork and pull request, step by step

Everything happens in the browser; no cloning needed.

1. Sign in to GitHub and open the [course repository](https://github.com/sr320/course-fish546-2026).
2. Click **Fork** (top right), keep your own account as the owner, and click **Create fork**. You now have a copy at `github.com/your-username/course-fish546-2026`.
3. In your fork, click `roster.md`, then the pencil icon (**Edit this file**).
4. Add one row below the example, in the same format:

   ```text
   | Your Name | https://github.com/course-fish546-2026/your-repo | RNA-seq |
   ```

   For the track, use the same one you picked on your Project Proposal issue: RNA-seq, eDNA, Methylation, Variants, Annotation, or Other. A provisional choice is fine.
5. Click **Commit changes…**, write a short message such as `Add Your Name to roster`, and commit directly to `main` in your fork.
6. Back on your fork's main page, click **Contribute** → **Open pull request**. Check that the base is `sr320/course-fish546-2026` `main` and the diff shows only your one added line, then click **Create pull request**.

If GitHub reports a conflict with someone else's line, leave it; we resolve those together on Thursday.
:::

## Project Proposal

Refine your Project Proposal issue this week: research question, data source, platform, and a draft endpoint. The proposal is provisional. Examples of strong draft endpoints:

- RNA-seq: a differential-expression result linked to treatment, environment, tissue, or life stage.
- eDNA / metabarcoding: a taxon-by-site or taxon-by-time summary with contamination caveats.
- DNA methylation: a methylation difference connected to genome annotation or regulatory context.
- Variants: a filtered variant summary, PCA, or population comparison.
- Annotation / discovery: candidate genes, contigs, or markers supported by sequence-similarity evidence.

## Assessment

Scored with the [weekly entry rubric](../how-we-work.qmd#weekly-entry-rubric). The Analysis criterion looks for an auditable search and a biologically reasoned interpretation, not merely a top hit.
